newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--U.S. GDP grew faster in Q1 '97 vs Q4 '96.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--U.S. GDP grew faster in Q1 '97 vs Q4 '96.

text.p: A robust U.S. economy probably grew more rapidly in the first three months of 1997 than in the fourth quarter of 1996, primarily because consumers grabbed their pocketbooks and went shopping, analysts said.

The initial look at first quarter U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to show the economy expanded at a 4.1 percent annualized pace after growing 3.8 percent in the prior period. Data are due out Wednesday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Consumer spending rose 3.4 percent in the fourth quarter.
By contrast, I.D.E.A. Inc senior economist David Sloan predicted it soared 5.9 percent in the first quarter.
Sloan said: "Basically, the most important factor is that wage growth is picking up. Employment growth is strong. People are feeling more secure in their jobs. Confidence is high."

"So, the underlying consumer fundamentals are good," Sloan said. Consumer spending was also boosted by milder-than-normal winter weather in January and February and by some earlier-than-usual tax refunds, he added.
Consumer spending is the main engine that drives the U.S. economy, representing some two-thirds of GDP.
Besides consumer spending, experts cited several other factors that contributed to a lesser extent to first quarter economic growth.

"The investment sector is no slouch this time," said Carol Stone, a senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc. She forecast gains in business and housing investment, government purchases, and business inventories.

In the fourth quarter, business investment rose 5.5 percent, housing investment fell 1.8 percent, government purchases and investment declined 0.9 percent and business inventories climbed $17.3 billion.
Net exports at -$98.4 billion had subtracted from GDP in the fourth quarter as imports outpaced exports.
Analysts predicted net exports were also a drag on economic growth in the first quarter.
Indeed, HSBC Markets' forecast called for slower GDP growth of 3.3 percent in the first period, according to Christopher Low, a senior economist at the firm.
"The imports are going to be the only real negative in this report," Low said. "And because of that, I think people are going to look at final sales of domestic product."
Final sales of domestic product climbed 4.9 percent in the fourth quarter.
For his part, I.D.E.A.'s Sloan said he expected exports to show a strong gain but that will be outweighed by an even stronger rise in imports.
He predicted net exports will be -$130.3 billion in the first quarter.
Sloan said his calculations show first quarter GDP should be up 5.6 percent excluding net exports.
